title: Backus–Naur form — Wikipedia
why: Best short account of where BNF came from: Backus's 1959 metalanguage for IAL/ALGOL 58, its formalisation in the ALGOL 60 report, and Naur's naming of it.

title: Context-free grammar — Wikipedia
why: States the context-free property in one sentence (a single nonterminal on the left that is rewritten regardless of its surroundings) and dates the formalism to Chomsky in the mid-1950s.

locator: §3.2.2 Context-Free Grammars, CONTEXT-FREE GRAMMARS box, printed p. 90
claim: EaC defines a context-free grammar as a quadruple (T, NT, S, P) in which T is the set of terminal symbols, or words, of the language L(G), and the terminals correspond to the syntactic categories the scanner returns.
quote: Formally, a context-free grammar G is a quadruple (T, NT, S, P) where: T is the set of terminal symbols, or words, in the language L(G). Terminal symbols correspond to syntactic categories returned by the scanner.

locator: §3.2.2 Context-Free Grammars, CONTEXT-FREE GRAMMARS box, printed p. 90
claim: In the same definition, NT is the set of nonterminals, which EaC calls syntactic variables giving abstraction and structure to the productions, and S is a nonterminal designated as the start or goal symbol.
quote: NT is the set of nonterminal symbols. They are syntactic variables introduced to provide abstraction and structure in the productions of G. S is a nonterminal symbol designated as the start symbol or goal symbol of the grammar.

locator: §3.2.2 Context-Free Grammars, CONTEXT-FREE GRAMMARS box, printed p. 90
claim: In EaC's definition the fourth part, P, is the set of productions or rewrite rules, and each rule replaces a single nonterminal by a string of one or more grammar symbols.
quote: P is the set of productions or rewrite rules in G. Each rule in P has the form NT → (T ∪ NT )+ ; that is, it replaces a single nonterminal with a string of one or more grammar symbols.

locator: §3.2.2, Derivation entry and the paragraph that follows, printed pp. 90–91
claim: EaC defines deriving a sentence as starting with a prototype string holding just the start symbol, then repeatedly picking a nonterminal in that string, choosing a rule for it, and rewriting it, until only terminal symbols remain.
quote: To derive a sentence, we start with a prototype string that contains just the start symbol. We then repeat the following process: (1) pick a nonterminal symbol, α, in the prototype string; (2) choose a grammar rule, α → β; and (3) rewrite α with β. When the prototype string contains only terminal symbols, the derivation halts.

locator: §3.2.3 More Complex Examples, printed p. 92
claim: EaC says the leftmost and rightmost derivations of one sentence use the same rules in a different order, and that because a syntax tree records which rules were applied and not their order, the two derivations have identical parse trees.
quote: The leftmost and rightmost derivations use the same set of rules; they apply those rules in a different order. Because a syntax tree represents the rules applied, but not the order of their application, the parse trees for the two derivations are identical.

locator: §3.2.3, Ambiguity sidebar, printed p. 92
claim: EaC calls a grammar G ambiguous when some sentence in L(G) has more than one rightmost (or leftmost) derivation, or equivalently more than one parse tree.
quote: A grammar G is ambiguous if some sentence in L(G) has more than one rightmost (or leftmost) derivation. Alternatively, a grammar G is ambiguous if some sentence in L(G) has more than one parse tree.

locator: §3.2.3, printed p. 92
claim: EaC's reason for rejecting ambiguity is that a program must have a single meaning, or the compiler cannot know what code to generate.
quote: A program must have a single meaning; otherwise, the compiler cannot know what code to generate. Thus, ambiguity is a bad property in a programming language.

locator: §3.2.3, printed p. 93
claim: EaC notes that under the straightforward if–then–else grammar the sentence "if Expr1 then if Expr2 then Other1 else Other2" has two distinct rightmost derivations.
quote: The grammar shows that the else clause is optional. Unfortunately, the sentence if Expr1 then if Expr2 then Other1 else Other2 has two distinct rightmost derivations.

locator: §6.8.4.1 The if statement, Semantics, clause 3
claim: C11 settles the dangling else in the semantics of the if statement, not in its grammar: an else is associated with the lexically nearest preceding if that the syntax allows.
quote: An else is associated with the lexically nearest preceding if that is allowed by the syntax.

locator: §6.5.6 Additive operators, Syntax, clause 1
claim: C11's grammar gives the additive-expression productions as a multiplicative-expression, or an additive-expression followed by + or - and a multiplicative-expression, so the additive level is written in terms of the multiplicative level below it.
quote: additive-expression: multiplicative-expression additive-expression + multiplicative-expression additive-expression - multiplicative-expression

locator: §6.5 Expressions, footnote 85
claim: C11's footnote 85 says the syntax itself specifies operator precedence, in the order of the major subclauses of §6.5 with the highest precedence first, so the operands of binary + are the expressions of 6.5.1 through 6.5.6.
quote: The syntax specifies the precedence of operators in the evaluation of an expression, which is the same as the order of the major subclauses of this subclause, highest precedence first. Thus, for example, the expressions allowed as the operands of the binary + operator (6.5.6) are those expressions defined in 6.5.1 through 6.5.6.

locator: History, paragraph before "BNF itself emerged", Wikipedia Backus–Naur form, rev 1380042613
claim: Wikipedia's BNF article says Noam Chomsky adapted Thue's rewriting formalism to natural language syntax and in 1956 introduced the distinction between generative rules, which are those of context-free grammars, and transformation rules.
quote: Noam Chomsky, teaching linguistics to students of information theory at MIT combined linguistics and mathematics, adapting Thue's formalism to describe natural language syntax. In 1956, he introduced a clear distinction between generative rules (those of context-free grammars) and transformation rules.

locator: History, paragraph starting "BNF itself emerged", Wikipedia Backus–Naur form, rev 1380042613
claim: Wikipedia's BNF article says BNF emerged when John Backus proposed a metalanguage of metalinguistic formulas for defining the syntax of IAL, now known as ALGOL 58, in 1959.
quote: BNF itself emerged when John Backus, a programming language designer at IBM, proposed a metalanguage of metalinguistic formulas to define the syntax of the new programming language IAL, known today as ALGOL 58, in 1959.

locator: History, paragraph starting "BNF itself emerged", Wikipedia Backus–Naur form, rev 1380042613
claim: According to the same paragraph, the notation was formalized in the ALGOL 60 report and Peter Naur named it Backus normal form in the committee's 1963 report.
quote: This notation was formalized in the ALGOL 60 report, where Peter Naur named it Backus normal form in the committee's 1963 report.

locator: §3.2.1 Why Not Use Regular Expressions?, printed p. 88
claim: EaC shows an RE that matches any correctly parenthesized expression but also matches wrong ones such as "a + ( b × c" and "a + b ) × c )", and concludes that no RE matches all expressions with balanced parentheses.
quote: Unfortunately, it also matches many syntactically incorrect expressions, such as “a + ( b × c” and “a + b ) × c ).” In fact, we cannot write an RE that will match all expressions with balanced parentheses.

locator: §3.2.1 Why Not Use Regular Expressions?, printed p. 88
claim: EaC calls the inability to match brackets of any kind a fundamental limitation of REs, because the recognizers behind them cannot count, having only a finite set of states.
quote: The inability to match brackets, be they ( ), { }, or begin and end is a fundamental limitation of REs; the corresponding recognizers cannot count because they have only a finite set of states.

locator: §3.2.2, Sentential form sidebar, printed p. 90
claim: EaC's sidebar defines a sentential form as a string of symbols that occurs as one step in a valid derivation.
quote: a string of symbols that occurs as one step in a valid derivation

locator: §3.2.3, Leftmost derivation sidebar, printed p. 92
claim: EaC's sidebar defines a leftmost derivation as a derivation that rewrites the leftmost nonterminal at each step.
quote: a derivation that rewrites, at each step, the leftmost nonterminal

locator: §6.5.5 Multiplicative operators, Syntax, clause 1
claim: C11's grammar gives the multiplicative-expression productions as a cast-expression, or a multiplicative-expression followed by *, / or % and a cast-expression.
quote: multiplicative-expression: cast-expression multiplicative-expression * cast-expression multiplicative-expression / cast-expression multiplicative-expression % cast-expression

locator: Formal definitions, leading definition sentence, Wikipedia Context-free grammar, rev 1374572485
claim: Wikipedia's definition says the production rules of a context-free grammar can be applied to a nonterminal symbol regardless of its context.
quote: In formal language theory, a context-free grammar (CFG) is a formal grammar whose production rules can be applied to a nonterminal symbol regardless of its context.

locator: Formal definitions, second paragraph, Wikipedia Context-free grammar, rev 1374572485 (math fallbacks left as the fetched text writes them)
claim: Wikipedia says that no matter which symbols surround it, the single nonterminal on the left hand side of a context-free rule can always be replaced by the string on the right hand side.
quote: Regardless of which symbols surround it, the single nonterminal A[{\displaystyle A}] on the left hand side can always be replaced by α[{\displaystyle \alpha }] on the right hand side.
